name: Evidence summary: plasma ctDNA fragmentomics workflows
description: Plain-language summary of what the reviewed evidence shows. Draft until reviewed.

attributes.value: Eight sources compare plasma cfDNA fragmentomic workflows on retrospective case-control cohorts. None is a prospective screening study and none measures clinical benefit. Cristiano et al. 2019, the DELFI developers, report 73% sensitivity (152 of 208 cancers) at a reported 98% specificity for DELFI in repeated cross-validation against 215 healthy individuals. Hou et al. 2024 re-implemented ten published fragmentation patterns and DELFI with one support vector machine each on the same cohort. They are independent of every pattern except IFS, which their corresponding author developed. In 10 x 10-fold cross-validation, pan-cancer AUC within open chromatin regions ranged from 0.8741 (fragment length) to 0.9736 (5' end motif), and their DELFI re-implementation reached 0.9575. Rankings changed on independent cohorts. On 46 lung cancers and 385 healthy individuals, with a model trained on 12 lung cancers, the end-motif model fell to AUC 0.5355 and sensitivity 0.0652 at 95% specificity, while fragment size distribution reached 0.9386 and 0.7174. Hou et al.'s supplementary pan-cancer and liver cancer sensitivities conflict with other tables of the same file and are not shown. Wang et al. 2026, the UNITE developers, stratified cancers by ichorCNA tumour fraction in pooled public and new 0.1x data that include samples of the DELFI and Jiang et al. cohorts used above. For cancers with an estimated tumour fraction of 3% or less, cross-validated AUC was 0.878 for all five features combined, 0.873 for fragment length, 0.857 for the SD of length counts, 0.736 for copy number, 0.715 for the C/T end-motif ratio and 0.651 for the short/long ratio, against 0.603 for a classifier using the ichorCNA tumour fraction alone, which detected 0.058 of these cancers at 95% specificity. For cancers with an estimated fraction above 3% and up to 10%, the ichorCNA classifier reached 0.983, above the combined model (0.962) and copy number alone (0.926). The extracted UNITE tables give sensitivity at a fixed specificity only for the ichorCNA comparator; the fragmentomic models' values are in a sheet not yet extracted. Jamshidi et al. 2022 (Cancer Cell), by the GRAIL developers, scored fragment length and fragment endpoint classifiers from 30x cfDNA whole-genome sequencing on the same CCGA substudy 1 participants as their methylation, copy-number and variant classifiers, at a 98% specificity threshold set post hoc within each set. On the validation set of 464 cancers and 362 non-cancers the fragment length classifier detected 29% (95% CI 25% to 34%) and the fragment endpoint classifier 18% (15% to 22%), against 34% for whole-genome methylation analysed double-blinded; both fragment classifiers were developed after the validation set had been unblinded, so these are not blinded validation results, and no tumour-fraction-stratified sensitivity is printed. Zeng et al. 2026 (Nature Cancer), by the cfMeDIP-seq developers, computed fragmentomic features from cfMeDIP-seq reads, which are enriched for methylated fragments rather than drawn from whole-genome sequencing, and report means over 10 fold models. On an independent paired-end validation set, a fragment-ratio classifier reached AUC 0.848 and detected 0.533 of cancers at 99% specificity, and fragment ratios combined with methylation reached 0.954 and 0.766. The validation set has 17 healthy controls, so its 99% specificity allows no false positive among them, and Li-Fraumeni syndrome carriers without current cancer count as cancers in its sensitivities. Three of the five classifiers that include end motifs scored below AUC 0.5 there, which the authors attribute to healthy controls processed with a different laboratory protocol, so validation results for all five are not shown. Helzer et al. 2025 (Nature Communications) compared twelve fragmentomic metrics adapted to targeted exon panels, including the authors' own fragment-size entropy metrics, their combination and Griffin, with one classifier and shared folds, on plasma from patients with metastatic cancer. The healthy-versus-cancer one-vs-rest AUROC ranged from 0.835 (open-chromatin entropy) to 0.989 (first-exon depth) in a UW cohort of 404 cancers and 27 healthy donors, with Griffin at 0.944, and from 0.951 to 1.000 in public GRAIL panel data from 151 cancers and 47 healthy donors. In a developer comparison on 0.1x whole-genome sequencing (Cell Reports Medicine 2026), a fragment-level language model (Fragmentia-AI) reached AUC 0.9561 on a held-out set of unstated size, against 0.9209 to 0.935 for the developers' re-implementation of DELFI features and 0.881 to 0.8863 for Griffin features under three classifiers. The same company's whole-genome model (Molecular Biomedicine 2026), on an independent test cohort of 2,952 cancers and 3,044 non-cancer controls, reached AUC 0.910 for cancers with an ichorCNA tumour fraction below 3% and detected 0.46 of them at a cutoff set to 98% specificity in training (observed test specificity 0.97); among those low-fraction cancers it detected 0.391 at stage I/II (637 of 1,628) and 0.708 at stage III/IV (345 of 487). Its tumour-fraction strata are ichorCNA estimates, no comparator was run on its cohorts, and its training cohort has the same number of non-cancer controls (1,245) as the Cell Reports Medicine cohort, so the two studies may share samples. Three of these four studies report on their authors' own method, and in the fourth the authors' own entropy metrics are among those compared. Cohorts, feature implementations, classifiers and validation designs differ, so no value is comparable across sources.

name: Evidence summary: plasma ctDNA methylation detection workflows
description: Plain-language summary of what the reviewed evidence shows. Draft until reviewed.

attributes.value: Six bounded sources compare cfDNA methylation methods. None is a prospective screening study and none measures clinical benefit. Jamshidi et al. 2022 (Cancer Cell), by the GRAIL developers, compared prototype cfDNA classifiers on the same CCGA substudy 1 participants at a 98% specificity threshold set post hoc within each set. On the validation set of 464 cancers and 362 non-cancers, analysed double-blinded, the whole-genome bisulfite methylation classifier detected 34% of cancers (95% CI 30% to 39%; 158 of 464), against 33% for variants with white-blood-cell correction, 30% for copy number with that correction, 27% for copy number, 16% for uncorrected variants and 2.6% for clinical risk factors alone; only the gap to the corrected variant classifier was not marked as significant. Among 127 validation cancers detected by all three representative classifiers, a methylation origin classifier developed after unblinding assigned the correct tissue for 75% (95 of 127), against 41% for copy number and 35% for corrected variants, with 'other' counted as correct for six cancer types. These are case-control results from the assay developer, not screening performance. Sun et al. 2024 (Genome Biology), an independent benchmark whose authors did not develop the tools, deconvolved real plasma with five methods and reported the ROC-AUC of a random forest trained on the estimated cell-type fractions; the paper does not state how the random forest was validated, so the AUCs may be in-sample. For 24 liver cancer patients and 32 healthy individuals (WGBS), AUCs were 0.96 (CelFEER), 0.93 (CelFiE), 0.91 (MethAtlas), 0.77 (cfNOMe) and 0.72 (UXM). On cfMethyl-Seq plasma (30 to 67 patients per cancer type, each against the same 193 healthy individuals), AUCs ranged from 0.72 (UXM, lung squamous cell carcinoma) to 0.93 (CelFiE, gastric cancer), and no method was highest for every cancer type. Giuili et al. 2025, a bioRxiv preprint not yet peer reviewed, ran ten reference-based tools inside the authors' DecoNFlow pipeline on in silico mixtures of tumour tissue or cell-line reads in healthy plasma reads. CelFiE had the lowest overall median tumour-fraction limit of detection in each dataset: 0.0070 (WGBS-TT), 0.0100 (RRBS-TT) and 0.0010 (RRBS-CL). CIBERSORT and EpiDISH had overall medians of 0.1000 to 0.2500 on WGBS-TT and RRBS-TT. For five tools the RRBS-CL values disagree between the supplementary table and Figure 4A and are not shown. Nguyen et al. 2023 (eLife), by the developers of the SPOT-MAS assay at Gene Solutions, compared three tissue-of-origin classifiers on combined methylation, fragment-length, copy-number and end-motif features from cancer patients only. In the validation cohort of 239 patients, overall accuracy was 0.53 (random forest), 0.69 (deep neural network) and 0.69 (graph convolutional network); the graph network was trained with the validation samples in its graph. Zeng et al. 2026 (Nature Cancer), by the cfMeDIP-seq developers, compared a cfMeDIP-seq methylation classifier with fragmentomic features of the same reads and their combinations, reporting means over 10 fold models. In cross-validation on 356 cancers and 64 healthy donors, methylation alone reached AUC 0.986 and detected 0.949 of cancers at 99% specificity; on an independent validation set its sensitivity at 99% specificity was 0.633, against 0.766 for methylation combined with fragment ratios. These sensitivities are read on few healthy controls (six or seven per cross-validation fold and 17 in the validation set), so 99% specificity there allows no false positive among them, and Li-Fraumeni syndrome carriers without current cancer count as cancers in the validation sensitivities. The Source Data give the methylation-only validation AUC as 0.694 and the text as 0.674, so that value is not shown. Xu and Feng 2026, a medRxiv preprint not yet peer reviewed, by authors who did not develop CpGPT, fine-tuned the CpGPT methylation foundation model on public targeted bisulfite cfDNA data from 254 gastrointestinal cancers and 46 non-cancer controls and built four classical classifiers themselves. On three train/validation/test splits with test partitions of about 30 samples, mean test AUROC was 0.9904 for CpGPT against 0.9573 (SVM), 0.9420 (elastic net), 0.8460 (gradient boosting) and 0.8408 (random forest); the candidate CpGs were selected using all 300 samples, including the test partitions. Neither study reports performance in a screening population. Tissue-of-origin evidence here comes from two developer studies, one methylation-only classifier scored on already detected cancers and one multimodal workflow, and neither classifies people without cancer.

attributes.value: RhoMax, which adds structural binding-pocket inputs, had the lowest wavelength error on each of its own wild-type holdout splits. In separate Rewire runs on the FLIP2 split, two amino-acid composition probes outranked two frozen ESM-2 probes, and both ESM-2 probes fell below a constant control. Averaged over four RhoMax splits, mean absolute error was 10.45 nm for RhoMax, 13.46 nm for RhoMax plus retinal and 14.90 nm for the BLASSO comparator, with standard deviations of 10.9 to 11.7 nm; per-split RhoMax error ran from 7.28 to 16.68 nm. In electronvolts the three methods are closer, and on split 3 all three print the same mean absolute error of 0.045 eV. On the FLIP2 Rhomax by_wild_type split of 184 held-out sequences, Rewire's runs gave a Spearman correlation of 0.418 for a 40-feature amino-acid composition probe and 0.418 for a 22-feature one, against -0.146 for a frozen ESM-2 8M probe and -0.222 for a 35M probe; NDCG was 0.955, 0.955, 0.896 and 0.907 against 0.921 for a training-mean control, whose Spearman is undefined. The two split definitions are different and their scores must not be pooled. The RhoMax values are reported by its authors with no independent reproduction, and the Rewire runs are single runs with no seed variability, with the 35M checkpoint chosen after the 8M outcome was known.

name: Evidence summary: tumour DNA somatic SNV and indel calling
description: Plain-language summary of what the reviewed evidence shows. Draft until reviewed.

attributes.value: Eight studies are linked, and their values cannot be pooled: truth sets, sequencing, caller versions and scoring scripts differ. Values are rounded to two decimals, except where the source prints percentages. In the Lancet developers' own virtual-tumour test, Lancet and Strelka2 both reached SNV F1 0.85, with indel F1 0.81 and 0.77. Wang et al. 2020 ran eight callers, NeuSomatic and their own majority-vote ensembles on eight whole-genome tumour-normal pairs, with older caller versions (for example MuTect2 from GATK 3.7). An ensemble had the highest SNV F1 on seven of the eight pairs; on DREAM set 4, NeuSomatic, whose model was trained on DREAM set 3, was highest at 0.86. The best single configuration reached SNV F1 0.92 to 0.96 on the simulated DREAM sets 1 to 3 but 0.70 to 0.81 on the CLL, AML and MB tumours, where most callers had precision below 0.6 against curated truth sets that the authors say may be incomplete, so precision there is a lower bound. Indel F1 on the CLL and MB tumours and the COLO829 cell line (AML has no indel truth set) was at most 0.72 for every configuration. Guille et al. 2025, who did not develop the callers, scored them on a WES replicate of the SEQC2 HCC1395 cell line (1,160 truth SNVs, 50 truth indels); another replicate with the same truth set was used to choose their ensembles. Leaving out DeepSomatic and NeuSomatic, whose pre-trained models were built with HCC1395 data, the best single caller reached SNV F1 0.85 (Mutect) and indel F1 0.66 (VarNet), and the authors' ensembles reached 0.88 for SNVs and 0.75 and 0.74 for indels. Strelka reached SNV F1 0.64 there, with precision 0.51, against 0.85 for Strelka2 in the Lancet test, which shows how much results depend on the study. Sahraeian et al. 2022, the NeuSomatic developers, scored callers on SEQC2 HCC1395 whole-genome data in the half of the genome held out from their model training: 21 replicate pairs from six centres, 47 tumour purity and coverage mixtures, and six library preparations. Their NeuSomatic and NeuSomatic-S models trained on SEQC2 data (SEQC-WGS-Spike, SEQC-WGS-GT-50 and SEQC-WGS-GT50-SpikeWGS10) and Octopus-RF, whose random forest is not identified, are left out because they were built from the same cell line or may have been. Among the rest, mean F1 over the 21 replicates was 92.3% for DRAGEN, 91.8% for NeuSomatic with its DREAM3 model and 89.0% for Strelka2 for SNVs, and 81.7%, 79.3% and 72.8% for indels. Over the purity and coverage mixtures (10x to 300x, 5% to 100% tumour), mean SNV F1 was at most 67.7% (Octopus with hard filters). With 5% tumour in an 80x normal, SNV F1 for a pure tumour fell from 88.6% to 43.8% for MuTect2 and from 93.3% to 47.8% for Lancet, but only from 92.4% to 90.9% for Strelka2. Hasan 2026, a single-author preprint run under the author's own company by someone who developed none of the callers, scored Mutect2, Strelka2, DeepSomatic and three ensembles defined by the author on the GIAB HG008 tumour-normal pair against a draft truth set of clonal and truncal variants; the original scoring code was not retained. In the primary region (14,014 truth variants, excluding sites with germline interference), F1 was 0.91 for a two-of-three majority vote, 0.90 for Mutect2 and DeepSomatic and 0.78 for Strelka2; for indels Mutect2 reached 0.82 and DeepSomatic and Strelka2 0.69. Over the whole draft benchmark, F1 was 0.70 to 0.79 for all six. Two developer papers tested tumour-only calling, without the matched normal this use case assumes, so they are linked as proxy evidence. On Illumina COLO829 at 50x, ClairS-TO's developers report SNV F1 0.77 for ClairS-TO against 0.62 for DeepSomatic, 0.58 for Mutect2, 0.40 for Octopus and 0.22 for Pisces, with indel F1 at most 0.29; each F1 is at the threshold that gave that caller its best F1 on the test data, and truth variants with fewer than three supporting reads or VAF below 0.05 in the tested data were not scored. The VarNet-T developers report SNV AUPRC 0.77 for VarNet-T on SEQC2 and 0.66 on COLO829, against 0.54 and 0.27 for ClairS-TO and 0.08 and 0.07 for Mutect2; on three low-burden tumours every tumour-only caller had AUPRC at most 0.11. The two papers used different COLO829 sequencing data and truth sets: the same ClairS-TO model (Illumina SSRS, v0.4.0) had COLO829 SNV AUPRC 0.65 in its developers' paper and 0.27 in the VarNet-T paper. On a synthetic WES pair, where inserted SNVs make precision near 1 by construction, Mutect2 recalled 0.63 of inserted SNVs and Strelka2 0.46 with default nf-core/sarek settings. Only the HG008 preprint reports interval estimates; no linked study covers FFPE tissue, ctDNA or targeted panels, and none establishes clinical performance.

attributes.value: Four comparisons join the Seraseq reference and paediatric NCH cohort evidence; values cannot be pooled across studies. Tamura et al. 2026 ran 12 short-read callers on haematologic cancer cell lines; one, Genomon, comes from a co-author's group. On 61 driver fusions in conventional RNA-seq of 170 cell lines, Arriba detected all 61 (TPR 1), FusionCatcher 0.98, STAR-Fusion 0.93, InFusion 0.43 and STARChip 0.41. On 24 driver fusions in targeted RNA-seq of 26 cell lines, Arriba again reached 1 and STAR-Fusion 0.92, InFusion 0.17 and STARChip 0. A driver fusion entered these truth sets only if at least four callers, including the one scored, found it and it had literature or RT-PCR support, so fusions that most callers miss are under-represented and these values may overstate sensitivity. Against a consensus of the other callers, the number of single-caller calls, a measure of review burden, ranged on conventional RNA-seq from 327 for TrinityFusion-D and 1,061 for STAR-Fusion (PPV 0.39) to 9,567 for Arriba (PPV 0.08), 22,445 for FusionCatcher and 695,295 for Pizzly. On nanopore long reads from 51 paediatric B-ALL samples (Lin et al. 2026), scored on the dominant fusion per sample, JAFFAL reached sensitivity 0.76, LongGF 0.70 and FusionSeeker 0.63, with precision 0.79 to 0.95; the authors' own FUSILLI reached 0.81. At about one eighth of the depth, sensitivity was 0.09 to 0.27. In an independent long-read benchmark (Dorney et al. 2026 preprint), no caller exceeded F1 0.35 on 400 simulated fusions at 100 Gb and 95% read identity: CTAT-LR-Fusion 0.35 (recall 0.28, precision 0.46), JAFFAL 0.29, Genion 0.20, FusionSeeker 0.14, GFSeeker 0.07 and LongGF 0.04. On all ONT PCR-cDNA reads of the MCF7 cell line, CTAT-LR-Fusion's calls matched 20 of 53 previously reported fusions, with 51 other calls; JAFFAL matched 19 with 38 other calls and FusionSeeker 11 with 359. The other calls mix real fusions missing from the literature list and false calls. On the Huh7 cell line, pooling six long-read callers per long-read platform and three short-read callers for Illumina, PacBio Kinnex recovered 20 of 34 previously reported fusions, ONT PCR-cDNA 17 and Illumina 15. Against karyotyping, FISH and RT-PCR in 101 adult and paediatric acute leukaemia patients (Kim et al. 2026), an Arriba workflow with manual review detected 40 of 48 conventionally detected fusions (sensitivity 83.3%) and called fusions in 21.4% of 56 conventionally negative results; these count against specificity, although the authors describe several as well-known recurrent fusions and confirmed one by RT-PCR and Sanger sequencing. These are cell lines, simulations and leukaemia samples: no linked comparison covers solid-tumour specimens, FFPE tissue or novel-fusion discovery, only Kim et al. score against orthogonal clinical assays, none reports interval estimates, and none establishes clinical performance.
